and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

# PRODUCT.md

# Baste

## Register

product

## Users

Designers and developers building interfaces for people with specific cultural influences. The Studio is a workroom for editing personas, fitting design tokens, collecting references and generating assets; the public site explains the method.

## Product Purpose

Turn films, music, spaces, tools and obsessions into usable, culturally specific UI assets. Explore diverse candidates and retain a useful archive, rather than collapsing the process into a single answer.

## Brand Personality

Tactile, attentive, particular. The existing house style is a tailor's atelier: pattern paper, ink, thread and chalk. Keep its quiet framing so a persona's own palette remains legible.

## Anti-references

Generic demographic personas, interchangeable AI asset galleries, decorative controls that obscure the fitting process, and account or payment states that imply access before it is verified.

## Design Principles

- Cultural influences are the measurements; demographics alone do not determine a fitting.
- Preserve diverse options and show useful production states.
- Reuse the established atelier components and tokens.
- Keep local work, provider credentials and hosted account state understandable.
- Show verified availability, failures and next actions in the flow where they matter.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Preserve the existing semantic forms, keyboard focus, skip links, readable text contrast and reduced-motion alternatives. Keep controls usable on narrow screens with accessible names when labels collapse.

This context records the existing AGENT_REFERENCE.md, Panda tokens and Studio component conventions; it does not introduce a new visual direction.

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check specific claims or fields against their evidence;
  send uncertain or failing cases to a person or reasoning model. Explore
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).
- **Respond to changing state.** Code can retain goals and observations while fresh
  judgments guide the next bounded step. Keep inferred state distinct from observed
  facts, and check freshness before applying a result to a changed situation.

For open-ended requests, offer the few directions that best serve the user's goal
and recommend a starting point. For a concrete request, choose the relevant pattern
and build; a brainstorm is not a mandatory detour.

## Design the judgments

Choose by what the answer means, then read the relevant primitive page:

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

Give each question enough relevant **state** to answer: source text, identities,
relationships, policies, and current facts. Prefer named JSON fields when context
has several parts. Put the judgment in **instructions** and define its possible
answers in **criteria**. Question IDs are for code and are not sent to the model;
include complete meaning in the question. Reference nested state with backticked
paths such as `ticket.messages[0].text`.

Ask one narrow, coherent judgment per question. Split independently useful dimensions,
without destroying the relationship being judged. A bounded action selection or
contextual interpretation is valid; atomic does not mean literal fact extraction
or a one-sentence limit. Strings work for simple questions. Use structured objects
or arrays when definitions, contrasts, exclusions, or examples clarify instructions
or criteria. Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own.

Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit;
use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful. For source-value
selection, check candidate coverage: the model cannot choose an omitted value.

## Compose and verify

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful
speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.
State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.
A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,
construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;
measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.

Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on
the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution
concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near
0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several
acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not
invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.

Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating
preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a
weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings
are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models
are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.

Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,
inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed
outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.
Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal
rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.
"}}

## Editorial review for documents

Review the writing before final formatting, and repeat the relevant checks after substantial revisions. Use the examples below to identify the problem and rewrite the actual document. Apply a suggested rewrite only when the source and section support its meaning. Do not borrow dates, roles, results, or other facts from an example.

### Read headings as an outline

Read the document title and section headings together without the body text. They should identify the subject, scope, and organization of the document. Check that each heading describes what its section actually contains. Reconsider a vague heading's framing before polishing individual words, and keep a good existing heading when it already does the job.

| Wording to improve                  | Clearer wording when supported by the section |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Performance that frames the choice  | 2025 and 2026 Performance Metrics             |
| From oversight to trusted execution | AI Policy Approval Process                    |
| Reported outcomes with limits       | Pilot Results and Study Limitations           |

Use a plain subject label for background, definitions, or process descriptions. Use a factual finding as a heading only when the section establishes that finding. Follow the title and heading rules in `SKILL.md`, preserving punctuation only when a name or established term requires it.

### Use paragraphs to explain relationships

Give each paragraph a clear point and explain how its facts or actions relate. The document should make sense without a presenter supplying missing connections. Use complete sentences and vary their length naturally. When a sentence bundles actions, explain their sequence or dependency when the source supports it.

For example, the fragments "Policy approval required. Legal approves the policy. Publication follows approval." become "Legal must approve the policy before publication." The rewrite preserves the actor and approval condition while making their relationship clear.

Use lists for distinct items readers need to identify, follow, or compare. Keep a useful list of three items when all three matter. Avoid adding filler to complete a trio or repeatedly using the same three-part rhythm. Do not invent an owner, sequence, or causal link to make vague source material sound more concrete.

### Unpack compressed labels and unnecessary compounds

Replace dense modifiers and abstract labels with natural phrases that state the intended meaning. Rewrite the phrase rather than simply deleting its hyphens.

| Compressed wording           | Clearer wording                   |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Approval-ready evidence pack | Evidence required for approval    |
| Decision-enabling insights   | Findings relevant to the decision |

Use the first rewrite for a section listing approval requirements. If the original phrase describes a completed packet, preserve that status with "Evidence ready for approval." A clearer label must still express the intended meaning.

Preserve official names, defined terms, and established technical vocabulary when precision requires them. Explain an unfamiliar term on first use when the audience needs it, then use it consistently. In body text, keep ordinary grammatical hyphens when they clarify meaning.

### Preserve the claim when simplifying

Check the rewrite against the source. Keep numbers attached to their units, comparison baseline, and time period. Preserve conditions and uncertainty, including the distinction between "may," "should," and "must." Keep recommendations separate from findings and associations separate from causal claims.

| Source wording                                            | Edit to avoid                       | Safer wording or action                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Costs may fall if volume increases                        | Higher volume lowers costs          | Costs may fall with higher volume                                                                      |
| Transit use recovered to 79 percent of its previous level | Transit use increased by 79 percent | Transit use reached 79 percent of its previous level                                                   |
| A structurally lower level of commuting                   | A permanent drop in commuting       | Retain the structural claim or explain the underlying change using the source; do not infer permanence |

When the original is ambiguous, consult the source or retain the uncertainty. Do not silently choose a stronger interpretation, add a result, or remove a qualification to make the prose sound decisive.

### Use punctuation and voice in context

Prefer active voice when the actor is known and relevant. Use passive voice when the action or result deserves emphasis or the source does not identify the actor. Do not invent an actor solely to eliminate a passive construction.

Use punctuation in body text to make relationships and qualifications clear. Revise repeated punctuation used to manufacture emphasis or rhythm. Apply these checks in context rather than banning every instance of a construction. The title and heading rules in `SKILL.md` still apply, including their exception for punctuation required by names or established terms.

### Write for human readers

Follow user instructions first. Preserve the style of an existing document or supplied reference.

1. Read the request and source files. Identify the author, the recipient, and what the document must help the recipient understand or do.
2. Decide what kind of document is needed: a letter, memo, report, proposal, procedure, form, or another requested format. Choose the structure for that use.

L19: # Confidence
L20: 
L21: How TypeSafe reports certainty, how it differs from probability, and how to use it to control system behavior.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: All Score and Choice answers from TypeSafe include a `probabilities` property representing the probability distribution across the options (for Choice) or levels (for Score). The shape of that distribution is what tells you how certain the model is: concentrated on one outcome means a confident answer, spread out means an uncertain one. The answer’s `confidence` property collapses that shape into a single number from 0 to 1, so you can threshold on it without doing the math yourself.
L25: (Noul answers don’t carry one.)
L26: ##
L27: 
L28: cite3†​ L29: 
L30: Confidence is derived from the probabilities
L31: 
L32: `confidence` is a statistic computed from the probability distribution the answer already gives you. TypeSafe computes it for you and returns it on every Choice and Score answer, so the common case needs no extra work on your side.
L33: A solid default: We provide `confidence` as a convenient measure that fits most use-cases, but you are never locked into our definition. Depending on what you are evaluating, a different measure may serve you better, which is exactly why we give you the full `probabilities` in the response. The pros and cons of different computations is a specialized topic that we’ll keep to a separate cookbook rather than this page, and will add the link here when we do!
L34: For a cite4†Choice , the distribution is `probabilities` across your options. For a cite5†Score , it is the distribution across your levels. In both cases a flatter distribution means lower confidence: low confidence on a Choice often means none of the options are a clear winner over the others, and low confidence on a Score often means the levels are ambiguous, multi-dimensional, or the state doesn’t contain enough to go on.
L35: ##
L36: 
L37: cite6†​ L38: 
L39: ”I don’t know” is a useful signal
L40: 
L41: If an intelligent system, whether human or machine, cannot express honest uncertainty, the system cannot be trusted. Confidence gives you a built-in mechanism for the model to say “I’m not sure about this one.” This lets your code implement different behavior for different levels of certainty, which is the foundation for building systems you can actually rely on.
L42: ##
L43: 
L44: cite7†​ L45: 
L46: Three paths for using confidence in your code
L47: A useful starting pattern is to divide confidence into three ranges, each producing a different system behavior: High confidence: Act automatically. The model has a clear read and you can proceed without human involvement. Medium confidence: Proceed with caution. The model has a reasonable answer but is not certain. Depending on context, you might ask the user to confirm, flag for review, or gather more information before acting. Low confidence: Do not act.
L48: Route to a human, request clarification, or fall back to a different system. The model is telling you it does not have enough information or the question is not a good fit. Where you draw those boundaries depends on the stakes.
L49: ##
L50: 
L51: cite8†​ L52: 
L53: Thresholds scale with risk
L54: A confidence threshold is not one number. Different actions within the same system should be gated at different levels depending on the consequences of getting it wrong.
L55: 
L56:     `response = client.system_one(
L57:         state=user_message,
L58:         questions={
L59:             "action": Choice(
L60:                 instructions="What is the user trying to do?",
L61:                 criteria={
L62:                     "check_balance": "View account balance",
L63:                     "approve_transfer": "Approve the pending withdrawal request",
L64:                     "support": "Get help with an issue",
L65:                 },
L66:             ),
L67:         },
L68:     )
L69: 
L70:     action = response.answers["action"]
L71:     confidence = action.confidence
L72: 
L73:     if confidence < 0.5:
L74:         # Model is genuinely unsure. Don't guess.
L75:         route_to_human(user_message)
L76: 
L77:     elif action.choice == "check_balance":
L78:         # Low stakes. Showing the wrong screen is recoverable.
L79:         show_balance(account_id)
L80: 
L81:     elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
L82:         if confidence > 0.9:
L83:             # High stakes, high confidence. Proceed with confirmation.
L84:             confirm_then_execute(account_id)
L85:         else:
L86:             # High stakes, moderate confidence. Verify first.
L87:             ask_user_to_confirm(account_id)
L88:     `
L89: The 0.5 confidence floor catches anything the model reports as genuinely uncertain. Above that, the threshold for acting without confirmation is higher for a destructive operation than for a read-only one. Your code encodes the risk tolerance.
L90: 
L91: The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case. Start with conservative thresholds, test with your own data, and adjust as you observe results.

L19: # Composite scoring
L20: 
L21: Break a complex judgment into atomic scores, combine with weights you control in code.
L22: 
L23: Copy page Copy page
L24: 
L25: Oftentimes we want to rank a set of items based on several criteria at once. Composite scoring is an easy way to think about this: break the judgment into independent dimensions, score each one separately, and combine them with weights you control in code.
L26: ##
L27: 
L28: cite3†​ L29: 
L30: Example: resume screening
L31: 
L32: Let’s imagine you are processing resumes for engineering roles. You want to rank the candidates based on several criteria, and ultimately select the top X candidates for further review.
L33: 
L34: ###
L35: 
L36: cite4†​ L37: 
L38: Step 1: score each dimension independently
L39: ###
L40: 
L41: cite5†​ L42: 
L43: Step 2: combine with weights
L44: 
L45: Each dimension is normalized to 0–1 and weighted. The weights give you an easy way to adjust the relative importance of each dimension, without losing any of the nuance of the individual scores.
L46: scoring.py
L47: 
L48:     `py      = response.answers["python_depth"].score / 4
L49:     lead    = response.answers["team_leadership"].score / 4
L50:     arch    = response.answers["system_design"].score / 4
L51:     general = response.answers["generalist"].score / 4
L52: 
L53:     # Senior IC
L54:     ic_score = (0.40 * py) + (0.10 * lead) + (0.40 * arch) + (0.10 * general)
L55: 
L56:     # Engineering Manager
L57:     em_score = (0.15 * py) + (0.40 * lead) + (0.20 * arch) + (0.25 * general)
L58:     `
L59: This gives you the ability to rank the candidates based on the composite score. But more importantly, it gives you visibility into how exactly the final score is being calculated. If the highest ranking candidates are not matching your expectations, you can adjust the weights to find the right balance.

The requested partner can reuse Baste’s asset and account foundations, but it needs a new project/conversation layer. Current personas describe the intended audience; they are not yet persistent conversational characters.

| Area | Existing extension point | Current limit / recommended addition |
|---|---|---|
| Persona | `src/persona/types.ts:12`, `builder.ts:13`, `store.ts:55` | Culture, influences, behaviors, aesthetic. Add a separate `DesignPartner` referencing a persona: portrait, authored personality, likes/dislikes, speaking style, voice identity, revision. Keep audience persona and partner identity distinguishable so “both perspectives” has a clear meaning. |
| Hosted ownership | `src/notorganic/scope.ts:4`, `personas.ts:10`, `src/gui/api.ts:1139` | Authenticated DID controls `AsyncLocalStorage`; files live under `.baste/accounts/<sha256 DID>/`. Reuse this boundary for projects, partners, messages, evidence, jobs and histories. Never accept a browser-supplied owner DID. |
| Opening three options | `src/persona/builder.ts`, `src/assets/generators.ts:130`, `src/generation/qd.ts` | No character-generation flow. Create a persisted candidate batch containing exactly three varied partner definitions from brief/persona. Generate portraits through the existing image service. Selecting one atomically records all candidate trait snapshots plus selected ID, activates it, discards other candidates from active project state and cancels unfinished work. Asset QD diversity is separate from choosing one conversational partner. |
| Agent/conversation | `.flue/agents/baste.ts:17` | Initializes a Flue agent/session, then does a plain action switch; session is unused. No chat, tool loop, message storage, interruption, streaming or conversational memory. Build reusable server command services and a bounded tool loop; Flue can become an adapter to that runtime. |
| Tool catalog | `src/mcp/server.ts:45` | Tools exist for personas, token/prompt generation, decomposition, remix, brand kits, import/export. They use the unscoped local store. Hosted conversation tools must call account/project-scoped services directly; do not pass through these handlers unchanged. |
| GUI capabilities | `src/gui/api.ts:178`, `:455`, `:515`, `:556`, `:618`, `:793`, `:907`, `:967` | CRUD, tokens, moodboard, feedback, OpenPencil edits, decomposition, remix, splitting are reusable functions after extraction from route handlers. Add typed commands with validation, revision checks and history; use them from agent, GUI and MCP alike. |
| Live site evidence | `src/decompose/index.ts:78`, `:142`; `src/shared/url.ts:65` | Plain mode extracts HTML/CSS. Deep mode optionally imports Playwright, calls `goto/content/url`, then closes the browser. No screenshots, persistent navigation, authenticated sessions, viewport state or action evidence. Playwright is not in root dependencies. |
| Critique | `src/evaluation/typesafe-judge.ts:136` | Jev explicitly gets **text-only** persona, prompt, metadata and optional SVG source. Its five scores plus pet-peeve gate are useful policy primitives; they cannot inspect pixels or establish rendered quality. Add a visual observation stage, then typed Jev judgments over grounded observations, then natural partner commentary. |
| Speech | `src/notorganic/server.ts:7`, `:116` | No voice/audio path or playback UI. Implement persisted provider voice identity and an opt-in conversation playback mode first; each reply can have a cancellable speech job. Realtime voice remains a distinct later transport. |
| History | `src/versioning/types.ts`, `database.ts:118`, `registry.ts:132`, `:320`, `:423` | SQLite semantic changes, components, branches, diffs and revert exist. No GUI history endpoint, project-wide transaction model or comprehensive event log. Reuse compatible token-diff utilities, but extend storage around project revisions and transactions. |
| Learning/analytics | `src/evaluation/feedback-memory.ts:15`, `src/gui/api.ts:556` | Asset ratings append account-scoped JSONL and feed recent preferences back to the judge. No product analytics. Add a typed decision event schema and an analytics projection containing decisions/traits only; conversation text, audio and screenshots stay out of analytics. |
| Frontend | `site/src/routes/gui/index.tsx`, `components/studio/{context,workspace}.tsx`, `site/src/lib/{api,api-types,demo-client}.ts` | Qwik/Panda studio is persona selection plus tabs. Shared store already refreshes on account identity change. Extend with project state, candidate selection, conversation, evidence and revision events. API contracts are duplicated on frontend, so introduce a shared schema package/module or generated contracts. |

Recommended new modules:

- `src/projects/{types,schema,store,commands,history}.ts`: durable project aggregate, optimistic revision checks, atomic command application, undo/revert.
- `src/partners/{types,generation,selection,prompt,voice}.ts`: three candidate generation, selected identity, two critique perspectives, controlled speaking style.
- `src/conversation/{store,runtime,tools,events}.ts`: persisted messages/tool calls, interruptible generation, streaming event protocol, idempotent requests.
- `src/evidence/{types,browser,store,observe}.ts`: connected sites, navigation sessions, screenshots, DOM/locator observations, capture timestamps and evidence references.
- `src/analytics/{events,projection}.ts`: allowlisted trait/decision telemetry and project-history projection.
- `site/src/components/studio/partner/*`: candidate opening, partner profile, fluid conversation/work surface, evidence viewer and project history.

A project should hold `id`, `owner`, `revision`, brief, source-persona reference, chosen partner, connected sites, design state, artifacts and active runs. Conversation messages and evidence should be separate persisted records, referenced by ID rather than repeatedly copied into the aggregate.

For “edit while collaborating,” each tool should apply a typed project command and return the resulting revision plus human-readable changes. The visible design updates from that event; the assistant’s reply explains what changed. Autosave and agent edits need revision conflict handling so a late tool result cannot overwrite a user’s newer edit. Every successful mutation should identify actor, message/tool call, changed entities, previous/new values and related evidence.

For connected browsing, retain explicit navigation state and capture desktop/mobile evidence after interactions. A useful evidence record includes URL, final URL, viewport, screenshot asset/hash, DOM excerpt/locator, action that reached the state, capture time and provenance. Page content is evidence, never tool authorization. The current deep-decomposition path bypasses `safeFetch` while navigating; a browser service must enforce destination/network restrictions for initial navigation, redirects and subresources.

For critique, use the sequence **browser evidence → visual observations → typed judgments → persona reply**. Let Jev assess audience fit, partner taste, pet-peeve violations and actionable priorities from observations that carry evidence references. Keep the two perspectives explicit in data even when the partner communicates naturally. The current text-only judge should continue labeling its evidence honestly.

Two current implementation details matter before building atop the existing history:

1. `src/gui/api.ts:618` imports OpenPencil edits primarily into BrandKit palette/font fields. It does not persist the complete edited token document as canonical design state.
2. It calls `registry.initPersona()` afterward (`:668`), which creates another initial version/theme/main branch (`src/versioning/registry.ts:67`), rather than recording the actual edited token diff. That path is not a complete undoable mutation system.

Hosted provider work is also required. Baste presently requests `wallet:read usage:read billing:checkout infer:image judgement:evaluate`; its server permits only account/models/wallet/checkout/images/judgement routes. Chat, vision and speech need real provider capabilities, registration/scopes, explicit server routes and corresponding bounded spending policy. Existing generation planning in `src/gui/api.ts:272` and budget reservation at `:318` provide a reusable pattern; current jobs live only in a process-local `Map`, so partner runs should become durable.

A practical build sequence is:

1. Shared schemas, project store, command/history layer and analytics event contract.
2. Three candidates, selection, portraits and editable partner profile.
3. Persisted conversation with streaming events and project tools.
4. Connected browser evidence and grounded dual-perspective critique.
5. Opt-in spoken replies.
6. Integrate the work surface, project history and analytics projection.

No files changed or tests run. Findings are from the current dirty working tree.

L27: Architecture
L28: # Architecture
L29: 
L30: Build dashboards, CRUD interfaces, and monitoring tools. The LLM generates the UI once, then your app runs independently.
L31: 
L32: Copy Markdown Open
L33: 
L34: ## cite26†The problem today L35: 
L36: In most AI-powered applications, when a user interacts with a generated UI (filtering data, submitting a form, refreshing a view), the request goes back through the LLM. The model re-processes the context, calls tools, and regenerates the response. Every click costs tokens. Every interaction adds latency.
L37: ## cite27†How OpenUI changes this L38: 
L39: OpenUI separates generation from execution. The LLM generates the interface once. After that, the UI runs on its own: fetching data, handling state, and responding to user actions without any LLM involvement.
L40: 
L41: cite28†Image: Architecture diagram showing two phases: GENERATE (one-time) and EXECUTE (ongoing, no LLM) L42: ### cite29†Generate L43: 
L44: The user describes what they want. Your backend sends the request to an LLM along with a system prompt that includes your component library and tool descriptions. The LLM responds with openui-lang code, a compact declarative format that describes the UI layout, data sources, and interactions.
L45: ### cite30†Execute L46: 
L47: The Renderer parses the generated code. When it encounters a `Query("list_tickets")`, the runtime calls your tool directly, no LLM roundtrip. When the user clicks a button that triggers `@Run(createResult)`, the runtime executes the mutation against your tool. When a `$variable` changes from a dropdown, all dependent queries re-fetch automatically.
L48: 
L49: The LLM generated the wiring. The runtime executes it.
L50: Keep this generation path reliable in production with streaming error correction and provider fallbacks.
L51: 
L52: cite31†Explore the Gateway L53: ## cite32†What this enables L54: 
L55:   * Reactive dashboards with date range filters, auto-refresh, and live KPIs computed from query results
L56:   * CRUD interfaces with create forms, edit modals, tables with search and sort
L57:   * Monitoring tools with periodic refresh, server health metrics, and error rate tracking
L58:   * Any tool-connected UI. If you can expose it as a tool (via cite33†MCP†modelcontextprotocol.io or function map), the LLM can wire it into a UI
L59: 
L60: Try it live: cite34†Open the GitHub Demo L61: ## cite35†Iterate and refine L62: The LLM doesn't have to get it right the first time. With cite11†incremental editing , the user says "add a pie chart" and the LLM outputs only the 2-3 changed statements and the parser merges them into the existing code. Existing queries, state, and bindings stay intact.
L63: 
L64:     `Turn 1:                              Turn 2 (patch only):
L65: 
L66:     root = Stack([header, tbl])          root = Stack([header, chart, tbl])  ← updated
L67:     header = CardHeader("Tickets")       chart = PieChart(["Open","Closed"], ← new
L68:     tickets = Query(...)                   [@Count(@Filter(..., "open")),
L69:     tbl = Table([...])                      @Count(@Filter(..., "closed"))
L70:                                            ], "donut")
L71:       20 lines, ~400 tokens               3 lines, ~60 tokens (85% fewer)`
L72: ## cite36†Connecting tools L73: 
L74: The Renderer accepts a `toolProvider` prop that tells the runtime how to call your tools. Two options:
L75: 
L76: Function map, a plain object of async functions:
L77: 
L78:     `<Renderer
L79:       toolProvider={{
L80:         list_tickets: async (args) => fetch("/api/tickets").then((r) => r.json()),
L81:         create_ticket: async (args) =>
L82:           fetch("/api/tickets", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify(args) }).then((r) => r.json()),
L83:       }}
L84:       response={code}
L85:       library={library}
L86:     />`
L87: cite33†MCP†modelcontextprotocol.io client for server-side tools:
L88: 
L89:     `import { Client } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js";
L90:     import { StreamableHTTPClientTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/streamableHttp.js";
L91: 
L92:     const client = new Client({ name: "my-app", version: "1.0.0" });
L93:     await client.connect(new StreamableHTTPClientTransport(new URL("/api/mcp")));
L94:     <Renderer toolProvider={client} response={code} library={library} />;`
L95: These examples are simplified for demonstration. In production, you'll need to handle authentication, error boundaries, and connection lifecycle.
L96: 
L97: The cite34†GitHub Demo uses a function map where tools run entirely client-side, calling the GitHub API directly from the browser. Server-side applications can expose the same tool surface through MCP.
L98: ## cite37†A concrete example L99: 
L100: Here's the full flow for a ticket tracker: define tools, generate the prompt, render the output.
L101: ### cite38†1. Define your tools L102: 
L103:     `// tools.ts
L104:     const tools: ToolSpec[] = [
L105:       {
L106:         name: "list_tickets",
L107:         description: "List all tickets",
L108:         inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {} },
L109:         outputSchema: {
L110:           type: "object",
L111:           properties: {
L112:             rows: {
L113:               type: "array",
L114:               items: {
L115:                 type: "object",
L116:                 properties: { title: { type: "string" }, priority: { type: "string" } },
L117:               },
L118:             },
L119:           },
L120:         },
L121:       },
L122:       {
L123:         name: "create_ticket",
L124:         description: "Create a new ticket",
L125:         inputSchema: {
L126:           type: "object",
L127:           properties: {
L128:             title: { type: "string" },
L129:             priority: { type: "string" },
L130:           },
L131:         },
L132:         outputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { success: { type: "boolean" } } },
L133:       },
L134:     ];`
L135: ### cite39†2. Generate the prompt and call the LLM L136: 
L137:     `// route.ts
L138:     import OpenAI from "openai";
L139:     import { generateSystemPrompt, type LibrarySpec } from "@openuidev/lang-core";
L140:     import componentSpec from "./generated/component-spec.json";
L141: 
L142:     const gateway = new OpenAI({
L143:       apiKey: process.env.THESYS_API_KEY,
L144:       baseURL: "https://api.thesys.dev/v1/embed",
L145:     });
L146: 
L147:     const systemPrompt = generateSystemPrompt({
L148:       library: componentSpec as LibrarySpec,
L149:       promptOptions: { tools, toolCalls: true, bindings: true },
L150:     });
L151: 
L152:     const completion = await gateway.chat.completions.create({
L153:       model: "openai/gpt-5",
L154:       stream: true,
L155:       messages: [
L156:         { role: "system", content: systemPrompt },
L157:         { role: "user", content: "Build a ticket tracker with a create form and table" },
L158:       ],
L159:     });`
L160: ### cite40†3. Render the response L161: 
L162:     `// page.tsx
L163:     <Renderer
L164:       library={library}
L165:       response={streamedText}
L166:       isStreaming={isStreaming}
L167:       toolProvider={{
L168:         list_tickets: async () => db.query("SELECT * FROM tickets"),
L169:         create_ticket: async (args) => db.query("INSERT INTO tickets ...", args),
L170:       }}
L171:     />`
L172: ### cite41†What the LLM generates L173: 
L174:     `$title = ""
L175:     $priority = "medium"
L176:     createResult = Mutation("create_ticket", {title: $title, priority: $priority})
L177:     tickets = Query("list_tickets", {}, {rows: []})
L178:     submitBtn = Button("Create", Action([@Run(createResult), @Run(tickets), @Reset($title, $priority)]))
L179:     form = Form("create", submitBtn, [
L180:       FormControl("Title", Input("title", $title)),
L181:       FormControl("Priority", Select("priority", $priority, [
L182:         SelectItem("low", "Low"), SelectItem("medium", "Medium"), SelectItem("high", "High")
L183:       ]))
L184:     ])
L185:     tbl = Table([Col("Title", tickets.rows.title), Col("Priority", tickets.rows.priority)])
L186:     root = Stack([CardHeader("Ticket Tracker"), form, tbl])`
L187: ### cite42†What happens at runtime L188: 
L189:   1. `Query("list_tickets")` → runtime calls your tool → table fills with data
L190:   2. User types a title, picks a priority, clicks "Create"
L191:   3. `@Run(createResult)` → runtime calls `create_ticket` directly
L192:   4. `@Run(tickets)` → runtime re-fetches `list_tickets` → table updates
L193:   5. `@Reset($title, $priority)` → form clears
L194: 
L195: All without the LLM.
L196: cite7†Reliability Build reliable LLM-generated interfaces by measuring, reducing, and correcting generation errors. cite9†Reactive State Make your UI interactive with $variables that update automatically. L197: ### On this page

Define your tools cite39†2. Generate the prompt and call the LLM cite40†3. Render the response cite41†What the LLM generates cite42†What happens at runtime --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L28: # Reactive State
L29: 
L30: Make your UI interactive with $variables that update automatically.
L31: 
L32: Copy Markdown Open
L33: 
L34: Every UI needs state: which tab is selected, what the user typed, whether a modal is open. In OpenUI Lang, state is declared with `$variables`.
L35: 
L36: ## cite26†Declaring a variable L37: 
L38: A `$variable` is a line that starts with `$`:
L39: 
L40:     `$days = "7"
L41:     $title = ""
L42:     $showEdit = false`
L43: 
L44: That's it. The value on the right is the default.
L45: ## cite27†Binding to inputs L46: 
L47: When you pass a `$variable` to an input component, it creates a two-way binding. The user changes the input, the variable updates. The variable changes, the input updates.
L48: 
L49:     `$days = "7"
L50:     filter = Select("days", $days, [SelectItem("7", "7 days"), SelectItem("30", "30 days")])`
L51: ## cite28†Using variables in expressions L52: 
L53: Any expression can read a `$variable`:
L54: 
L55:     `title = TextContent("Showing last " + $days + " days")
L56:     data = Query("analytics", {days: $days}, {rows: []})`
L57: 
L58: When `$days` changes (user picks "30" in the Select), the title updates and the Query re-fetches with the new value. This happens automatically - no wiring needed.
L59: ## cite29†Changing state from buttons L60: 
L61: Use `@Set` inside an `Action` to change a variable when a button is clicked:
L62: 
L63:     `btn = Button("Show 30 days", Action([@Set($days, "30")]))`
L64: 
L65: You can set multiple variables at once:
L66: 
L67:     `saveBtn = Button("Save", Action([@Set($showEdit, false), @Set($saved, true)]))`
L68: ## cite30†Resetting to defaults L69: 
L70: `@Reset` restores variables to their declared defaults:
L71: 
L72:     `$title = ""
L73:     $priority = "medium"
L74:     resetBtn = Button("Clear", Action([@Reset($title, $priority)]))`
L75: 
L76: After click: `$title` goes back to `""`, `$priority` goes back to `"medium"`.
L77: 
L78: ## cite31†Conditional rendering L79: 
L80: Use ternary expressions to show/hide UI based on state:
L81: 
L82:     `$showEdit ? editForm : null

+# Baste design partners
+
+Draft implementation plan, October 1, 2026. This develops the confirmed choices in [the recovered side conversation](design-partner-recovery.json) and the subsequent Clef, Popmelt and OpenUI discussion. It proposes new product behavior; it does not describe an implemented feature.
+
+Baste should introduce a character with a face, voice and particular taste, then let the designer work with that character inside a live design. The partner can explore references, point out what appeals to it, make changes through tools, compare the result and remember decisions. Conversation, visual evidence and editing share one work surface.
+
+## First experience
+
+1. **Describe the project.** Accept a conversational brief, an existing persona, a connected local project or a reference URL. Begin generating immediately from the available context; ask a focused follow-up only when it materially changes the direction.
+2. **Meet three possible partners.** Each gets a generated portrait, name, short introduction, cultural influences, a few specific likes and dislikes, and a sample reaction to the same design. The three should differ in meaningful taste and working style. Portrait jobs stream in independently with honest loading and retry states.
+3. **Choose one.** Persist the chosen character and voice identity. Remove the other two from active project state and cancel unfinished candidate work. Retain the selection event and candidate trait snapshots for the requested decision analysis. This selection is separate from the diverse archive of generated design assets.
+4. **Look together.** Open the connected design. The partner can navigate, scroll, inspect interaction states, capture a viewport or element, and collect references. Both parties can point to the same element. A reference site is browsable; editing a site requires its connected project or editing integration.
+5. **Discuss and change.** A comment such as “this feels too polished for me” is attached to the relevant design state. The partner can show alternatives, bring up a control, or apply a project change using the active collaboration permissions. Each actual edit creates a revision with an undo path.
+6. **Keep working.** The selected partner, project, conversation, evidence and decisions survive reloads. Spoken replies are an opt-in conversation mode, with playback and interruption controls. Full live voice follows after the text and spoken-reply workflow works well.
+
+Example: the user asks, “Why does this page feel wrong for you?” The partner highlights the glossy hero and explains that its finish conflicts with the tactile references they chose. An inline surface shows the current design and two alternatives, plus a texture control. Adjustments update the preview immediately. A committed edit updates the connected project, captures the result and leaves a readable revision in history.
+
+## Character and taste
+
+Keep an audience persona and a conversational partner as related, distinguishable records. The audience describes whom the design serves. The partner has a authored personality, cultural world, critical approach, speaking style and preferences. A partner may embody that audience while also helping with design craft.
+
+Critique therefore retains two perspectives in its data: “this suits my taste” and “this helps the intended user.” Their tradeoffs can be expressed naturally in conversation. A character's preference is an interpretation, not evidence from a real user study.
+
+Store explicit user decisions separately from inferred preferences and the character's initial traits. The partner can have consistent opinions and explain disagreement. It must also recognize that the user can deliberately choose a different direction. Generate the portrait from the authored character; do not derive personality from facial appearance. Keep portrait and voice identity stable across sessions and allow either to be changed without losing project memory.
+
+## Models and tools
+
+Use a common typed decision interface with capability-aware providers. Route work by the evidence required, then evaluate providers on Baste examples before fixing permanent defaults.
+
+| Responsibility | Proposed owner | Result |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Character creation, conversation and tool planning | Conversational model | Character records, replies and validated tool requests |
+| Visual comparison and style coherence | Clef adapter | Typed judgments over actual screenshots and references |
+| Preference interpretation, textual consistency and next useful action | Existing Jev adapter | Typed judgments over brief, decisions and grounded observations |
+| Portrait and design asset creation | Image generation tools | Persisted media with generation provenance |
+| Spoken replies | Speech tool | Cancellable audio tied to a specific reply and voice |
+| Navigation, editing, validation and persistence | Application tools | Observations, mutations, revisions and receipts |
+
+Clef's official hosted API supports embedded images alongside typed questions; it currently allows up to four images per request and does not accept remote image URLs. Baste therefore needs a capture and image-preparation stage, rather than passing a website URL as visual evidence. The released model returns decisions rather than free-form explanations. A conversational model explains the result using the same evidence. [Cloudflare API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/clef/), [model card](https://huggingface.co/Cloudflare/clef).
+
+Do not route every interaction through both judges. Use Jev for text decisions, Clef when pixels matter, and deterministic code for exact constraints. Independent questions about the same evidence can be batched. A second call is useful when its input depends on an earlier answer. Cache by evidence, persona revision, question version and model identity.
+
+## Seeing and judging a design
+
+The review loop is: **observe → ask focused questions → explain with evidence → change through tools → observe again**.
+
+Capture the URL, viewport, interaction state, image hash, time, project revision, relevant DOM elements and the actions that reached the state. A desktop hero, mobile menu and hover state are different observations. Results against old revisions become stale instead of attaching silently to the newest design.
+
+Useful visual questions include:
+
+- Which of these variants better matches the selected references, including an “equally suitable” or “insufficient evidence” outcome?
+- How consistent are the typography, spacing, imagery and materials with the chosen direction? Judge these dimensions separately.
+- Does this element violate a specific, recorded dislike?
+- Does the primary action remain visually prominent in this captured state?
+- Did this revision improve the intended quality while preserving the qualities already accepted?
+
+Use element candidates and screenshot crops to ground findings. Clef can choose among known elements or assess a proposed observation; it does not automatically return a reliable free-form critique or locate every issue. The conversational model can draft observations, but explanations must remain tied to captured evidence and actual judgment results.
+
+Keep cultural fit, coherence, novelty and usability visible as separate dimensions. Baste's existing weighted rubric remains configurable. Exact contrast, overflow, keyboard and functional checks stay deterministic. A visual model's confidence describes its answer distribution; Baste must measure agreement with user preferences before treating it as a reliable predictor. [TypeSafe confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence), [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring).
+
+Evaluate pairwise choices on held-out screenshots and user decisions. Check order reversal, repeated judgments, mobile and desktop states, unusual styles and incomplete evidence. Generic decision benchmarks do not establish skill at aesthetic judgment. Preserve useful disagreements and diverse design candidates rather than optimizing everything toward one average appearance.
+
+## Fluid interface
+
+Keep the live design central. The partner has a compact, persistent presence with portrait, text entry and voice controls. Discussion and tool results can attach to selected elements or expand inline. On narrow screens, use an anchored sheet with a clear return to the design. Preserve focus and in-progress edits when the interface changes.
+
+Start with a small component catalog:
+
+| Surface | Purpose |
+| --- | --- |
+| Partner choices | Compare the three initial characters |
+| Evidence annotation | Point at a captured element and explain a reaction |
+| Variant comparison | Compare current and proposed treatments |
+| Palette and type controls | Adjust actual design values with a live preview |
+| Reference board | Collect and relate visual references |
+| Revision comparison | Inspect changes and undo them |
+| Preference prompt | Resolve a meaningful taste question |
+
+OpenUI composes these application-owned components and connects them to tools. Reactive state keeps ordinary controls responsive without a new model call for every click. Incremental changes preserve the controls and values that still apply. Actual design edits pass through the project's mutation tools, so a newly generated control never masquerades as a completed code change. [OpenUI architecture](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/architecture), [reactive state](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/reactive-state), [incremental editing](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/incremental-editing).
+
+Keep Baste's Qwik/Panda stack and existing atelier identity. Evaluate a Qwik adapter around the framework-independent OpenUI core, including state subscriptions, query lifecycle, cancellation, action dispatch and component validation. Qwik support is adapter work, not a verified drop-in integration. Use one versioned component/tool contract rather than inventing a second generative UI grammar. Keep a normal static interface available if an emitted surface is invalid.
+
+Popmelt's documented pattern is valuable here: element-level conversation, direct manipulation, local project context and a remembered history of design choices. Explore an optional in-page companion for connected projects, backed by the same Baste commands, so work can happen both in Studio and on the running site. This plan uses those interaction ideas; it does not claim Popmelt itself is integrated or that its advertised behavior was tested. [Popmelt](https://popmelt.com/).
+
+## Tool and project contract
+
+Introduce durable, account-scoped `Project`, `DesignPartner`, `Conversation`, `Evidence`, `DecisionEvent` and `Revision` records. A project references its brief, selected audience persona, partner, connected sites, canonical design state, artifacts and active runs. Large evidence and conversation records are stored separately and referenced by ID.
+
+All surfaces call the same validated service commands: agent, Studio, generated UI, CLI and MCP. Proposed tool families are partner creation/selection, browser observation/navigation, reference collection, visual judgment, token/component edits, project patches, comparison/revert and speech. Tool schemas describe actual capabilities; the model cannot invent tools or obtain authority from page content.
+
+Mutations include a base revision and idempotency key, and return the resulting revision, changed entities and a human-readable result. Apply changes atomically where possible. For connected repositories, stage a bounded patch, verify it, apply it and capture the updated preview; retain enough history to undo the patch without overwriting later user edits. A failed or interrupted action retains an accurate status. Newer edits take precedence over stale tool results.
+
+The user's selected collaboration scope covers the connected project. The runtime still distinguishes project edits from external publication, payment and unrelated sites. Implement the browser as an isolated service with project-specific sessions, destination checks on navigation and subresources, and explicit capture/action history. Existing static decomposition is not this browser runtime.
+
+Not Organic remains the hosted identity, wallet and provider boundary. Extend its advertised capabilities, Baste's allowlisted routes and spending accounting for chat, visual judgment and speech. Credentials remain server-held. Budget a run across conversation, captures, judgments, media and speech, and stop further dispatch when cancelled or out of budget. The current image/Jev integration does not establish these new capabilities.
+
+## Learning from decisions
+
+Record candidate exposure and order, selection, preference answers, accepted edits, reversions and explicit reasons as typed events. Include relevant trait snapshots, evidence/revision IDs and model/rubric versions so a decision can be understood later.
+
+Project history retains the detailed work context. The product analytics projection contains decision events and traits, following the recovered choice; raw conversation, voice recordings, screenshots and provider credentials are excluded from that projection. A candidate selection is not a negative label for every trait of the alternatives. Distinguish explicit preference, inferred preference, no response and technical failure.
+
+Use these events first to improve ranking and measure usefulness: whether judgments match later choices, whether changes survive, and where users reverse the partner. Fine-tuning is a later experiment once there is enough representative, appropriately scoped evidence. Do not silently turn every logged event into a training example.
+
+## Existing foundations and gaps
+
+The source review found reusable foundations, but no complete conversational partner workflow:
+
+- `src/persona/types.ts`, `builder.ts` and `store.ts`: cultural persona records; add partner identity and project context around them.
+- `src/assets/generators.ts`: hosted image generation suitable for portrait jobs; add portrait-specific output and identity handling.
+- `src/evaluation/typesafe-judge.ts`: explicit text-only Jev evidence; add a multimodal decision adapter and reusable rubrics without claiming existing pixel inspection.
+- `src/notorganic/scope.ts` and account stores: reuse DID ownership for all new records and assets.
+- `.flue/agents/baste.ts`: currently action dispatch with an unused session, not a persisted conversational tool loop.
+- `src/decompose/index.ts`: static extraction and a short-lived optional browser path; add persistent observation/action sessions and browser network enforcement.
+- `src/versioning/`: semantic changes and diffs; extend this into complete project revisions. The current OpenPencil import does not preserve the complete edited design as a reversible project mutation.
+- `src/mcp/server.ts` and `src/gui/api.ts`: extract shared commands before allowing hosted partners to use them; current local MCP handlers are not account-scoped.
+- `site/src/components/studio/`: preserve the existing components, but introduce a project work surface and shared generated contracts instead of extending duplicated API types indefinitely.
+
+Twyne references to reuse as patterns are `src/components/onboarding/conversational-interview.tsx` for progressive briefing, `src/utils/personas.ts` for character voice and critical method, `src/components/in-flow/catalog.ts` and `src/utils/in-flow-tools.ts` for bounded tool surfaces, and its flow/review and brief-history utilities for visible state and durable decisions. Twyne's existing cast does not already implement generated partner identities. These are current source references, including work in progress, rather than proof of deployed behavior.
+
+## Build sequence and acceptance
+
+| Stage | Deliverable | Acceptance evidence |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| 1. Shared foundation | Project/partner schemas, ownership, commands, revisions, event contract and hosted capability design | Account isolation; reload persistence; stale-write rejection; exact edit/undo round trip |
+| 2. Meet and talk | Three persisted candidates, generated portraits, selection, stable personality and streamed conversation | Choose one, reload, resume with the same character and recorded choice; generation failures recover individually |
+| 3. Look together | Connected browser, captures, element references, Clef adapter and Jev decisions | Navigate a real site, capture desktop/mobile states, receive grounded judgments and reject stale evidence |
+| 4. Collaborate | Initial OpenUI catalog, live controls, token/component tools and connected source patches | Discuss an element, adjust it through a generated surface, see the actual preview update, undo and reload without loss |
+| 5. Speak and learn | Opt-in spoken replies, cancellation, project decision history and analytics projection | Stable voice; stop playback/generation; retained decisions; analytics contains only its allowed event fields |
+
+After Stage 1, character/conversation, browser/visual judgment and the Qwik OpenUI adapter can proceed in parallel against the shared contracts. Stage 4 integrates them. The first complete release includes spoken replies; live duplex voice and broader project integrations follow later.
+
+The first acceptance journey is deliberately end to end: describe a project, meet three characters, choose one, open a connected site, discuss a specific element, compare an alternative, make and undo a real edit, hear an optional spoken reply, then reload and continue. Passing that journey is the release goal, rather than merely completing the individual adapters.

# Baste design partners

Draft implementation plan, October 1, 2026. This develops the confirmed choices in [the recovered side conversation](design-partner-recovery.json) and the subsequent Clef, Popmelt and OpenUI discussion. It proposes new product behavior; it does not describe an implemented feature.

Baste should introduce a character with a face, voice and particular taste, then let the designer work with that character inside a live design. The partner can explore references, point out what appeals to it, make changes through tools, compare the result and remember decisions. Conversation, visual evidence and editing share one work surface.

## First experience

1. **Describe the project.** Accept a conversational brief, an existing persona, a connected local project or a reference URL. Begin generating immediately from the available context; ask a focused follow-up only when it materially changes the direction.
2. **Meet three possible partners.** Each gets a generated portrait, name, short introduction, cultural influences, a few specific likes and dislikes, and a sample reaction to the same design. The three should differ in meaningful taste and working style. Portrait jobs stream in independently with honest loading and retry states.
3. **Choose one.** Persist the chosen character and voice identity. Remove the other two from active project state and cancel unfinished candidate work. Retain the selection event and candidate trait snapshots for the requested decision analysis. This selection is separate from the diverse archive of generated design assets.
4. **Look together.** Open the connected design. The partner can navigate, scroll, inspect interaction states, capture a viewport or element, and collect references. Both parties can point to the same element. A reference site is browsable; editing a site requires its connected project or editing integration.
5. **Discuss and change.** A comment such as “this feels too polished for me” is attached to the relevant design state. The partner can show alternatives, bring up a control, or apply a project change using the active collaboration permissions. Each actual edit creates a revision with an undo path.
6. **Keep working.** The selected partner, project, conversation, evidence and decisions survive reloads. Spoken replies are an opt-in conversation mode, with playback and interruption controls. Full live voice follows after the text and spoken-reply workflow works well.

Example: the user asks, “Why does this page feel wrong for you?” The partner highlights the glossy hero and explains that its finish conflicts with the tactile references they chose. An inline surface shows the current design and two alternatives, plus a texture control. Adjustments update the preview immediately. A committed edit updates the connected project, captures the result and leaves a readable revision in history.

## Character and taste

Keep an audience persona and a conversational partner as related, distinguishable records. The audience describes whom the design serves. The partner has an authored personality, cultural world, critical approach, speaking style and preferences. A partner may embody that audience while also helping with design craft.

Critique therefore retains two perspectives in its data: “this suits my taste” and “this helps the intended user.” Their tradeoffs can be expressed naturally in conversation. A character's preference is an interpretation, not evidence from a real user study.

Store explicit user decisions separately from inferred preferences and the character's initial traits. The partner can have consistent opinions and explain disagreement. It must also recognize that the user can deliberately choose a different direction. Generate the portrait from the authored character; do not derive personality from facial appearance. Keep portrait and voice identity stable across sessions and allow either to be changed without losing project memory.

## Models and tools

Use a common typed decision interface with capability-aware providers. Route work by the evidence required, then evaluate providers on Baste examples before fixing permanent defaults.

| Responsibility | Proposed owner | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Character creation, conversation and tool planning | Conversational model | Character records, replies and validated tool requests |
| Visual comparison and style coherence | Clef adapter | Typed judgments over actual screenshots and references |
| Preference interpretation, textual consistency and next useful action | Existing Jev adapter | Typed judgments over brief, decisions and grounded observations |
| Portrait and design asset creation | Image generation tools | Persisted media with generation provenance |
| Spoken replies | Speech tool | Cancellable audio tied to a specific reply and voice |
| Navigation, editing, validation and persistence | Application tools | Observations, mutations, revisions and receipts |

Clef's official hosted API supports embedded images alongside typed questions; it currently allows up to four images per request and does not accept remote image URLs. Baste therefore needs a capture and image-preparation stage, rather than passing a website URL as visual evidence. The released model returns decisions rather than free-form explanations. A conversational model explains the result using the same evidence. [Cloudflare API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/clef/), [model card](https://huggingface.co/Cloudflare/clef).

Do not route every interaction through both judges. Use Jev for text decisions, Clef when pixels matter, and deterministic code for exact constraints. Independent questions about the same evidence can be batched. A second call is useful when its input depends on an earlier answer. Cache by evidence, persona revision, question version and model identity.

## Seeing and judging a design

The review loop is: **observe → ask focused questions → explain with evidence → change through tools → observe again**.

Capture the URL, viewport, interaction state, image hash, time, project revision, relevant DOM elements and the actions that reached the state. A desktop hero, mobile menu and hover state are different observations. Results against old revisions become stale instead of attaching silently to the newest design.

Useful visual questions include:

- Which of these variants better matches the selected references, including an “equally suitable” or “insufficient evidence” outcome?
- How consistent are the typography, spacing, imagery and materials with the chosen direction? Judge these dimensions separately.
- Does this element violate a specific, recorded dislike?
- Does the primary action remain visually prominent in this captured state?
- Did this revision improve the intended quality while preserving the qualities already accepted?

Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/partner_plan_review
Payload:
No material issue. The plan preserves the recovered choices and the newer direction: three generated partners, stable portraits and personalities, tool-based site exploration and editing, Jev plus visual judgments, fluid OpenUI controls, and opt-in spoken replies.

It also identifies the required browser runtime, shared commands, reversible edits, Qwik adapter and hosted capabilities, with an end-to-end acceptance journey. New capabilities are consistently described as proposed and unverified.

I saved the full [Baste design partner plan](/home/diogenes/Projects/baste/docs/plans/design-partner.md), including the recovered choices and these new references.

The experience should feel like working beside a character with a particular eye:

- **Meet three partners**, each with a portrait, personality, cultural influences and distinct taste.
- **Choose one**, then develop the brief through conversation.
- **Explore designs together.** They navigate sites, inspect states and point to specific elements when expressing likes or dislikes.
- **Change things together.** Comparisons, palette controls and typography tools appear within the discussion. Changes reach the connected project, with history and undo.
- **Keep the relationship consistent.** Their voice, preferences and memory persist. Spoken replies are opt-in; live voice comes later.

I’d divide the intelligence between a conversational model that speaks and uses tools, **Jev for preference and workflow decisions**, and **Clef for judgments requiring actual pixels**. Clef’s hosted API accepts images, making screenshot comparisons feasible. Its usefulness for aesthetic judgment still needs evaluation against your choices. [Cloudflare documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/models/clef/).

**OpenUI is especially useful for making the conversation actionable.** If you discuss spacing, the partner can produce a spacing control; if you debate two treatments, it can produce a comparison. Those controls can call tools directly without regenerating the interface for every interaction. [OpenUI architecture](https://www.openui.com/docs/openui-lang/architecture).

The Popmelt influence I’d carry forward is **pointing, manipulating and discussing the actual design while retaining decision history**. That complements Twyne’s conversational approach well. [Popmelt](https://popmelt.com/).

The first complete milestone is: **choose a partner → inspect a connected site → discuss an element → compare alternatives → make and undo a real edit → reload and continue.** The plan is saved; this turn hasn’t implemented that feature.

settings.developer_instructions:
# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.

If explicit user input is required for another reason before progress can safely continue, do not use the `request_user_input` tool. Ask the user directly with one concise plain-text question instead. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.
